thread.title: Apple CEO Tim Cook's Words Come Back to Bite Him

title: Apple CEO Tim Cook's Words Come Back to Bite Him
text:
Apple CEO Tim Cook’s Words Come Back to Bite Him By Oct. 4, 2018 12:44 p.m. ET Order Reprints JOSH EDELSON/AFP/Getty Images Text size
It seemed like exquisite timing: Apple CEO Tim Cook dredged up the importance of user privacy and data in a TV interview this week that coincided with the latest security snafu at Facebook (FB) and news that Alphabet ’s (GOOGL) Google would finally address the topic in a White House meeting later this month.
Now, however, the timing couldn’t be worse. Apple reached a market value of $1 trillion on Thursday, propelled by the sustained success of the iPhone. WSJ's Spencer Jakab takes a look at how Apple got here. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal
An explosive Bloomberg Businessweek report claims Chinese operatives inserted tiny spy chips into motherboards used by major U.S. companies, including Apple (AAPL) and Amazon.com (AMZN). “Three senior insiders at Apple say that in the summer of 2015, it, too, found malicious chips on Supermicro motherboards,” according to the report. “Apple severed ties with Supermicro the following year, for what it described as unrelated reasons.”
Apple says it has “found absolutely no evidence” after internal investigations the past year following inquiries from Bloomberg.
Apple shares are down nearly 2%, to $227.51, in trading on Thursday.
No matter how one looks at it, the optics aren’t good.
In an interview with Vice News aired Tuesday , Cook forcefully invoked what has been a recurring theme of the company: Its unwavering commitment to “collect as little data as possible” and treat privacy as “one of the most important issues of the 21st century.”
Cook, as he has done for more than a year, chastised Facebook and Google —without directly naming them—for their reliance on data to sell advertising.
He didn’t stop there. Cook insisted Apple has not compromised user privacy in China despite criticism that its decision to begin hosting Chinese users’ iCloud accounts in a new data center within the country would give Chinese authorities easier access to text messages, email, and other data stored in the cloud.
“I wouldn’t get caught up in where’s the location of it,” Cook told Vice. “We have servers located in many different countries in the world. They’re not easier to get data from being in one country versus the next.”
Apple’s encryption policies, he vowed, are “the same in every country,” and the company has ultimate control over users’ data. Newsletter Sign-up
It’s all part of a longstanding strategy by Apple to differentiate itself from social-media rivals, as we reported in a Barron’s cover story . For the most part, the strategy has worked: In a year in which social-media companies have come increasingly under the scrutiny of regulators and investors, Apple shares are up 36%—easily outpacing Facebook (-10%), Alphabet (11%), and Twitter (TWTR) (17%).
But the Bloomberg report, on the heels of Cook’s TV lecture, underscores the pitfalls of doing business in China—where Apple gleans about 20% of its total annual revenue —while exalting one’s bona fides on privacy.
“The relationship between U.S. tech giants and China is very complex, and the nature of security threats and IP stealing is a real and worrisome issue in the Valley and across the board,” Daniel Ives, managing director of equity research at Wedbush Securities, tells Barron’s . “With consumers viewing their smartphone as a part of their everyday DNA, the worries around China chip hacking is a needle mover and one that can’t be brushed aside quickly from U.S. tech CEOs.”
